blocks.text: Reactions in which the reactants are completely consumed and converted into products are irreversible; they stop when the limiting reactant is used up. Some reactions, however, continue in both directions, forward and reverse, without changing the concentrations of reactants and products under the existing conditions; such reactions never stop and are called reversible reactions. When a reversible reaction takes place in a container that prevents the entry or escape of any substance involved, the quantities of the components change as some are consumed and others formed, until the reaction reaches chemical equilibrium: the concentrations of reactants and products become constant and the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal. Examples of reversible reactions, written with a double arrow, are N2 + 3H2 giving 2NH3, 2NO2 giving N2O4, and PCl5 giving PCl3 + Cl2.
The events of a reaction can be described at two scales: macroscopic events, which can be seen, and microscopic events, which cannot.
